comments.text:
"This wasn't some 5D chess mental gymnastics, this was a requirement."

Tying shoes isn't 5D chess mental gymnastics, either, but it's still done for a reason (like wanting to walk outdoors). There isn't a dichotomy between having to lower prices due to market conditions and having predicted the situation and so priced higher to avoid being forced to lower prices even further after Nvidia c***-blocked the lower price rather than the higher price. There is a calculation involved - a very simple, business-minded one.


That AMD was undercut by Nvidia's refreshes and so had to lower their prices isn't an argument that AMD didn't price higher to allow for a price-reduction later. That they would be required to lower prices to stay competitive after Nvidia reveal their refreshes at a price-point meant to undercut AMD is the reason why AMD would have priced higher initially. The reason why something happened isn't an argument against it having happened, and framing it as such is like arguing a thing's truth equals its invalidation.

comments.text:
I'll just offer up a cautionary tale: when I built my latest workstation during the peak of Covid a couple years ago, all I could get my hands on was the AMD Radeon RX 5700 XT from a local Best Buy. That spec sheet you're referring to implied that it would be a pretty decent fit for the AMD Ryzen 9 3900X for moderate 3ds Max rendering and decent modern gaming.

However, use cases have proven that not only was it a terrible match-up but I've concluded that this GPU is pure garbage overall. 3ds Max 2023 doesn't even hit the GPU, it just happily renders away with the CPU. The only time I've ever gotten the system to put any sort of load on the GPU is while developing in Unity for HDRP and, in those cases, the GPU ends up in thermal overload protection. It cannot and will not ever handle volumetrics and most decent games don't even recognize it for ray tracing.

I regret whatever it was I over-payed during Covid for this literal pile of useless trash. Am I being too harsh? I don't think so. It falls epically short in both gaming performance, rendering and in volumetric simulations. It, by default, has no Cuda cores and doesn't appear to have even heard of ray tracing and, to add insult to copious amounts of injury, it snowflakes out whenever presented with reasonable workloads, overheats and shuts down despite being PCIe 4.0. My son's NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1070 from many moons ago outperforms this GPU.

TLDR: It's overly-hyped junk. It cannot handle modern gaming and it fails to qualify as a recognizable GPU for moderate rendering tasks. DO NOT waste your cash on this trash.

comments.text:
Guys. 
Here’s a honest self review.
 
Pre-info: I’ve never got to really play with a high end Nvidia card, so I’m neither an Amd or Nvidia fanboy. The shop I bought the PC from is one of the most known in Europe, so don’t worry about the originality of the components..) 

Im playing on a 1080P 60hz Monitor. (!)

So... today I got my PC delivered 
(specs are: 
AMD Rx5700XT 50th anniversary ed.
AMD Ryzen 3600x
16 GB 3200 MHz g.skill aegis RAM 
B450M plus Max 
500 kingston SSD
1TB Toshiba HDD )

I started the PC, wondering the card wasn’t actually as loud as a lot of people claim it would be... but after I just clicked on Chrome, the graphics card just started directly to go up to about 1100 RPM... okay, still. The card wasn’t THAT loud. It was a bit annoying though, considering the fact that you might wanna spend some good time with the PC also writing word documents or something like that, it could be annoying having to listen to the graphics card as you don’t wanna put on headphones every time you use the PC. After that, the graphics card kept on spinning faster, and then slower again and again, without any purpose (I didn’t download anything, didn’t start anything, I did nothing). I think it went from about 1100 RPM down to 700 RPM and then straight up again. (MSI afterburner just showed 1100 RPM, but I could clearly tell by the sound the blower made that it spinned differently). I’m not a professional in PC gaming and components, so I didn’t really wanna mess the whole thing up by changing a lot of drivers and some undervolting, let it be afterburner custom settings... 

Next step: I started up a little mid gaming toaster test: Minecraft. And don’t get me wrong here, the RX5700XT was able to dominate the game, but don’t expect that you’ll run it on a 512x512 Sphax pure BD craft texture pack, it only runs at about 45-(sometimes)68 fps with medium Settings (chunks: 16, mip map 0). I next downloaded the SEUS shader and I was amazed. It was able to handle the shader with 16 chunks at 62-70 fps (some frame drops when moving into a new chunk, of course...) but I had the 512x512 texture pack in it AND the shader. (I think it was running way better because the card ran at 99%, without the shader it ran at ~50%) BUT also at 84 degrees, which is pretty hot, comparing it to other cards. So overall I could say the PC could handle Minecraft pretty good, if you don’t mind about the noise it made because it ran at a speed of 2100 RPM with shaders on... 

Next game, next chance: Fortnite.
I started up Fortnite, expecting the best results ever as many other vids claim it to be a very good experience. 
It was. 
The average fps was about 130-170 at epic settings, pretty astonishing in my opinion. But as I mentioned it in the Minecraft part, the card gets annoyingly noisy at 2100 RPM. (It sometimes even went up to almost 2300 RPM). 

So what’s my conclusion? 
My conclusion is, is that this card IS a good gaming card. You can mostly expect it to handle with games such as Fortnite, Minecraft, Metro Exodus, GTA V and so on.. but please... do me a favor: don’t even think about this Card Running at low RPM and not being loud just because you’re gaming at 1080P and not 1440P or 4K...
To be honest I’m really upset right now, I waited about a week for the PC, being totally amazed about turning it on and experience a whole new world of gaming and office work. 

I repeat it once, I’m not a Nvidia or Intel or AMD fanboy or whatever, this is a comment by some weird dude who was being too hurried to buy his first own PC system, but I wouldn’t even write a that long comment just to blame a company. 
 
Comments are welcome, I can answer your questions about the card until I send her back, that’ll be in about 3-5 days... 

R.I.P, my first ever gaming PC that more likely made me surprisingly upset rather than make me happy...

3. In every game comparison chart, the 5700XT (stock) BEAT both the RTX 2070 and the RTX 260 Super (Stock) where this card is positioned at cost-wise. I make a point to say STOCK because you very clearly made point that these drivers are Not Ready For PrimeTime and possibly could be hampered in its over-clocking numbers.
4. In many instances, the stock 5700XT is close enough to the RTX 2070 Super (a card priced $100 more) that we could expect performance parity in the near with future with driver updates.

First off, I really like how in-depth the reviews are from GN. But, I don’t believe that because GN staff like overclocking the bejesus out of computer hardware, its a best real world case assumption that the majority of people making these purchases will do similar. There’s a lot of people that just prefer to run cpus and gpus at stock speeds for either longevity of the product or, lack of technical expertise. 

I think it’s a better real world scenario to include performance tests at stock performance as well. As Scott said on PC World live stream, the cards are targeted towards the general population who are somewhat novices and just want to put the card in a system, load the drivers and do some gaming. Those who don’t want to worry about adequate case air flow for a axial type aib cooling solution heat exhaustion. It’s important to take notice of who AMD have marketed these blower style cards for.

Typical AMD GPU launch software issues. Oddly enough this doesn't worry me much as I'm not one who purchases hardware immediately on release. If they stick to the pattern this means that over time the drivers will mature and the cards true performance will be seen.

I'm not a "fanboy" but I'll probably wait about three months and get one of the AMD cards as the performance difference with my set up will be irrelevant and AMD's software interface for tinkering with the card is far, far superior to nVidia's. My requirements are modest enough that such a trivial difference is made into a legitimate enough creature comfort to effect my purchase.


Remember guys: Analyze your needs and potential upgrade path and buy accordingly. No need for a 2080ti if you're only playing at 1080p 60 with little interest or ability to upgrade beyond it.

comments.text:
@ps2232  I don't think Forza was that big of a deal. For one, it has been included in benchmarks ever since the game launched. There aren't a lot of racing games, and Forza seems one of the consistent ones across benchmarks. The only others I can think of are Project Cars, Dirt Rally and F1.
Forza could be seen as an outlier, BUT games like GTA5 and Fortnite can also be seen as outliers if they were included since Navi performs worse on those. So far they are the only games where Navi loses to the competition. So far in every single modern title Navi is at least equal to its competitor, but usually ahead by a noticeable margin.

Second, I've been going around the internet snatching up every single Navi review I could find and have put every single result in a spreadsheet (+30 games and over a dozen reviews). Overall, HWU Steve's results match up to everyone else's results. The 5700 is a clear win over the 2060 across the board with a steady 10% lead. On average the 5700XT is superior to both the 2060S and 2070 as well. And it's within spitting distance of the 2070S. In a few games it beats the 1080Ti, though those are rather rare.
With the 2060 as a baseline, this is how the others perform:
5700: 109.82%
5700XT: 123.95%
2060S: 113.06%
2070: 115.36%
2070S:131.34%
Had Navi kept its original MSRP of $380 and $450, it would still have remained the best value, albeit only slightly.

comments.text:
Still say it was a pre-planned price drop. Nvidia always undercuts AMD on performance because AMD is always late to the game. So, if AMD wanted to maintain a 45% margin (the Lisa Su tax) they had to price these cards after Nvidia released RTX Super. They couldn't announce these prices at E3 because Nvidia would have come down even more, and unlike Nvidia, AMD probably didn't have as much run to cut as Nvidia. AMD knew what performance range from Nvidia they were targeting and how much they planned to undercut that. But they also knew Nvidia would counter as they always do. AMD would have been stupid not to have learned this from their experience with Vega and Nvidia dropping the 1080ti and dropped the price of the GTX 1080  just as AMD was releasing Vega 64.

It has nothing to do with price to performance, but rather the highest possible justifiable margins. If it was about competing on price to performance, AMD would have release the RX 5700XT at closer to the likely $250-$300 (if that much) manufacturing cost considering these are not the first 7nm GPU AMD are releasing. Remember people claim the Radeon VII only exists because the RTX 2080 was priced as high as it was by Nvidia and Navi was delayed. AMD could do that because the Radeon VII came out of left field with everyone talking about Navi.

comments.text:
And another typical RTG launch...
The RDNA architecture seems to be pretty solid. It scales well, it doesn't seem to utterly collapse in poorly optimised games like GCN used to do and it flies in BF5. However, AMD had to screw it up with another round of "blowers blow" and drivers that are not ready. Especially the blower just pisses me off. Again, we have a GPU with such poor cooling that thermal throttling is an issue. Further we have Buildzoid is very deserved rage post from a month ago. This card will most likely use less power if you cap the boost clock to the same level and compare this reference POS. A cooler chip has less power leakage. That is a somewhat well known fact. Something the RTG does not understand. 
See: https://www.reddit.com/r/Amd/comments/byjy1t/amd_radeon_rx_5700_xt_picture_and_specs_leaked/eqihjy4/

With even a basic dual axial design, this card might have been limited to 200W TBP, with little to no performance loss. At 225W it very well could have been faster. That is how stupid these blowers are. Then from what I have been able to gather so far, the RX5700XT is hot clocked. Again a lot of voltage just to make the card a few precent faster. Because this work well with Hawai, Polaris and especially Vega. Why is the RTG incapable of just stepping to Sapphire and asking for a basic dual axial design? Why is this so difficult?

We need some competition in the GPU market and we need it badly. AMD finally brings something with a brand new architecture that is quite good, and then they screw up at the final step with a terrible cooler. The only thing that blowers bring are: louder, more power consumption and less performance. Something that won't be rectified in public perception because after launch day, most people who even look up benchmarks, will not understand what happened and will assume that the RX5700 series are just another round of "loud and hot"...
